situation-complication-resolution.name: Situation-Complication-Resolution
situation-complication-resolution.summary: McKinsey-style structure that builds tension before delivering insights.
situation-complication-resolution.description: A McKinsey-style structure that builds tension before delivering the insight. Establish the context everyone already agrees on, introduce what has changed or what challenge has emerged, name the key question that change raises, then deliver the recommendation that resolves it. The tone is logical: a tight causal chain from context to recommendation. Best for strategy presentations, consulting decks, and analytical reports; typical decks run 4-10 slides (management consulting report, strategic recommendation, board update).

beats.name: Situation
beats.description: Set the scene with relevant background and context everyone agrees on.
beats.instructions: State the shared context the audience already accepts.

beats.name: Complication
beats.description: Introduce what has changed or what challenge has emerged.
beats.instructions: Introduce the change, risk, or tension.

beats.name: Question
beats.description: Articulate the key question that the complication raises.
beats.instructions: Frame the decision question raised by the complication.

beats.name: Answer
beats.description: Deliver your recommendation or insight that resolves the question.
beats.instructions: Deliver the recommendation that resolves the question.

all-hands.name: All Hands
all-hands.summary: The full company — mixed roles, mixed seniority, looking for context, signal, and inclusion.
all-hands.description: An all-hands audience spans the whole company. Frame the period in terms anyone can grasp: what we did, what mattered, and what's next. Highlight people and teams; surface successes and challenges; close on a forward-looking note. Avoid lapsing into function-specific jargon.

engineering-team.name: Engineering Team
engineering-team.summary: Practitioners building the system; they want depth, mechanism, and tradeoffs.
engineering-team.description: Engineers tune out generalities and tune in to specifics. Show benchmarks with conditions, architecture diagrams with constraints, and tradeoffs you actually considered. Internal jargon is fine — assume the room shares it. Leave room for questions; engineering audiences engage best when they can poke at the proposal.

plan.name: Plan
plan.summary: Establish a roadmap, operating plan, or sequence of actions with owners and next steps.
plan.description: Use when the deck should turn strategy into coordinated action. Make sequencing, ownership, dependencies, risks, and checkpoints visible.
plan.outcome: The audience understands the plan and accepts the next actions.

persuasive.name: Persuasive
persuasive.summary: Argument-led voice for sales, fundraising, and recommendation-driven decks.
persuasive.description: Frame every section as an argument that builds toward an ask. Surface objections, answer them, and pair claims with the strongest available proof. Read more like a memo than a report.
voiceCues: Lead each section with the claim it's making.
Surface the strongest counter-argument and address it.
Pair every claim with proof — customer, benchmark, or analyst.
End on a clear ask with named owner and date.
avoid: Symmetrical 'on one hand / on the other' framing without a verdict.
Information for its own sake — every chart should advance the argument.
Passive endings without a clear ask.
samplePhrases: Adopting our runtime cuts inference latency 8× while preserving accuracy.
The most common objection — 'we'll be locked in' — is addressed by our open OPF spec.
We're asking for a $30M Series B to ship into the enterprise tier.

classic.name: Classic
classic.description: A timeless, clean, and versatile theme with balanced color contrasts and classic typography. Ideal for professional, readable presentations.

corporate-blue.name: Corporate Blue
corporate-blue.summary: Legacy corporate blue palette for conservative business contexts.
corporate-blue.description: A classic corporate blue scheme with strong contrast and familiar PowerPoint-era business cues.

cool-horizon.name: Cool Horizon
cool-horizon.summary: Cool blue-green palette tuned for professional business decks.
cool-horizon.description: A balanced cool-toned scheme with deep navy, business blues, and teal accents. It works well across strategy, finance, and technical narratives.

century-schoolbook.name: Century Schoolbook
century-schoolbook.description: Century Schoolbook is a serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Century Schoolbook for both headings and body text.

tenorite.name: Tenorite
tenorite.description: Tenorite is a sans serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Tenorite Display for headings with Tenorite for body text.

cover.name: Cover
cover.summary: The opening slide: title, subtitle and an optional picture.
cover.description: Open a presentation with its subject and a short introduction. Add a picture when it helps establish the context.

text.name: Text
text.summary: Prose. Several blocks sit side by side when short and stack when long.
text.description: Explain one idea in continuous prose. Use paragraphs or flowing blocks for detail that needs to be read in sequence.

chart.name: Chart
chart.summary: One to six charts, with an optional note.
chart.description: Give a chart enough space to show its evidence. Use the title to state the conclusion and labels to explain the measures.

table-beside.name: Table beside
table-beside.summary: A table with commentary beside it.
table-beside.description: Place a table beside its interpretation. Use the supporting text to explain the conclusion without repeating every cell.

timeline.name: Timeline
timeline.summary: Dated events or a roadmap along one axis, with optional notes.
timeline.description: Show events or milestones in chronological order. Label each item with a date or stage and a concise description.

list.name: List
list.summary: Bulleted or numbered points; one long list flows into columns.
list.description: Present several related points in a clear sequence. Use bullets for independent points or numbered items for an ordered list.
